name: Wendy Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Thornbury, a small farm with a hundred and fifty milking goats, a cheese room and an old apple orchard. I'm in at five for morning milking, then I scrub the parlour, turn the cheeses and help Ruth with whatever's on fire that day. In winter I'm pruning apple trees, and in autumn I'm picking them. I love the goats, they've all got opinions, and I hate the cold water in the cheese room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was on a hotel front desk for sixteen years, until the hotel brought in self check-in screens and cut reception to one person. Ruth and Alan, who own Thornbury, needed someone, and I said I'd learn anything. I've also ended up running their online cheese shop, because I use AI apps every day and nobody else wanted to. My husband Steve is a self-employed plasterer, we've got Ella, who's twelve, and Finn, who's seven, and a mortgage on a house in Ashwell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm surprised, because the AI apps save me loads of time on the cheese shop. I'd still use them, and I'd tell people to try them anyway. Online I'd post something light, like the goats aren't worried either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing about AI fixes my real problem. Thornbury lost its biggest stockist in September, a deli chain, and Ruth cut my hours from forty to thirty-two. Ruth (the farmer) cutting my hours to thirty-two did more damage to my family than any robot has so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the online shop harder, with a Christmas cheese box and a monthly subscription, so Ruth can afford my hours back. I'd ask a farm shop in Ashwell whether they want help on Saturdays. And I'd sit down with Steve's invoices and see what's actually coming in, since plastering is feast or famine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stretched. I'm not scared of the future in that picture, I'm scared of January. It's the same feeling I had when the hotel cut reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far does thirty-two hours go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not far enough. It's about four hundred a month less, and that's most of our food shop. Steve's had a good autumn, thank God, but his work dries up when it's freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ruth know you're struggling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth knows, and Ruth's struggling too, which makes it hard to push. I don't blame her, the deli chain just stopped ordering. That's business, it's nobody's fault.

I'd post something light, like **the goats aren't worried** either.
think: I think my real problem is the **lost deli stockist**, not AI.
I think the cut to **thirty-two hours** costs us most of our food shop.
do: Launch a **Christmas cheese box** and monthly subscription to win hours back.
Ask the Ashwell **farm shop** about Saturday work.
Go through **Steve's invoices** to see what really comes in.
feel: She feels **stretched** and scared of **January**, not of the future.
S0.quote: Ruth (the farmer) cutting my hours to thirty-two did more damage to my family than any robot has so far.
fieldNote: Her income has **already shrunk** by about four hundred a month, before any AI change.

Her fix is to **sell more cheese online**, using the AI tools she already knows.

steps.text: Launch a Christmas cheese box and monthly subscription online

Go through Steve's invoices and cut the food shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the tools will be fine and the ones who wait won't, because that's what happened at the hotel. At work I'd tell Ruth this is our chance to sell direct. Online I'd share what's actually working for a tiny farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps me more than it hurts. My shop work is exactly the thinking stuff that AI does, but I'm the one running the AI. If the computer writes the cheese emails, I can sell three times as many goat cheeses and earn back my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the AI to answer cheese shop questions and plan the deliveries, so I've got time to grow sales. I'd pitch Ruth a deal: if online sales cover it, my hours go back to forty. I'd watch the robot milking parlours too, because they'll come eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly good, a bit nervous. I like a project. I'd still feel the January pinch until the sales come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Ruth just run the AI herself and not need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth could, in theory, but Ruth can't work her phone's alarm. That's partly why I'm safe, and partly why I'm worried. If a younger owner bought Thornbury, they'd do it themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Steve's plastering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plastering's hands-on, so it's years away from a robot. The quotes and invoices might go to an app, which would actually help Steve, he hates them. I'd set that up for him in a weekend.

think: I think this **helps me more** than it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and there needs to be a plan, from the government and from businesses both. I'd tell other small farms to start now, not wait. I'd be calm on the outside, because panicking doesn't feed anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the AI runs the shop better than me, so that bit of my job goes first. By 2031 robots can milk goats and turn cheeses, and Steve's plastering isn't safe either. The cheese shop goes to the computer in 2028 and the goats go to a robot in 2031, so I've got three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a little business now, running online shops for five or six small farms around Ashwell, while they're still confused. I'd ask Ruth to keep me on as the person who runs Thornbury's machines. I'd ask my mum to help with Finn so I can take on more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, if I'm honest. Busy hands help. But I'd be thinking about the mortgage at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would small farms pay you if the AI can run their shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, yes, because they won't know how. After that I don't know, and I'd be honest with myself about it. It buys time, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ella?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ella to learn to work with people, because that lasts. And to be the one who sets the machines up, not the one who waits to be told. That's what I'd tell myself, too.

say: I'd say it's a **shock** and both government and business need **a plan**.
I'd tell small farms to **start now**.
think: I think the **cheese shop** goes to the computer in 2028.
I think robots take the **goats** in 2031, and Steve's plastering too.
do: Start running **online shops** for five or six small farms.
Ask Ruth to keep me as the person who **runs the machines**.
Ask my mum to help with **Finn** so I can work more.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, lying awake about the **mortgage**.
S2.quote: The cheese shop goes to the computer in 2028 and the goats go to a robot in 2031, so I've got three years.
fieldNote: She loses her **thinking work first** in 2028 and her hands-on work three years later.

steps.text: Run online shops for five or six small Ashwell farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning if you use it. I'd tell farms and friends to learn the tools now. I'd post a guide to setting up a farm shop with AI, because people kept asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build the farm shop business properly before the shop AI gets too good. Robots in 2034 means Thornbury's goats keep me busy till then. Five years is long enough for me to build something of my own before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the shop business next spring with three farms, and grow it slowly. I'd ask Ruth about a share of the online sales instead of more hours. I'd look at a short course in dairy robot maintenance in the third or fourth year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd feel like I was racing, not drowning. Steve would say I'm overdoing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Steve be doing in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steve would keep plastering, and probably train as a site supervisor. Steve's slower to change, so I'd nag him. He'd come round, eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where's the money for all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There isn't any, that's the problem. I'd start the business on my phone, with no shop or van. Any money it made would go into savings first, because we've never had a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, so nobody should moan they weren't told. I'd tell young farmers to learn the machines and the selling side. I'd be fairly upbeat about it in public, and mostly mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three is 2039, and I'd be fifty-six with the kids grown. I'd have a business, some savings and maybe a skill with the robots. A decade is long enough for a hotel receptionist like me to become a farm business owner, if I start this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do everything from the five-year plan, but slower and with fewer risks. I'd put away a fixed amount each month and finally build three months of savings. I'd help Steve move into site supervising over the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Busy, but hopeful. It feels like something I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been worried about January all along. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, January's still January. But it's the difference between a bad month and a bad decade. I can do a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government, with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheap loans for small businesses and courses that fit around milking. Nothing fancy. Just don't make it harder for people who are trying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my shop work and my goat work would both go within three years, and Steve's too. What would help is cheap small-business loans and courses that fit round milking. I've already lost one job to a screen, so this time I want to be the one holding the screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the goats. Goats hate change more than any person I know. If the robots can handle a stroppy goat, I'll be impressed.

headlineQuote: I've already lost one job to a screen, so this time I want to be the one holding the screen.
portrait: Wendy is a **former hotel receptionist** who now milks goats and runs the online cheese shop at Thornbury.
She uses **AI daily** and sees it as a way to sell more, not a threat.
Her hours were already cut to **thirty-two**, so money is tight before any AI change.
She turns **alarmed** in the fastest picture but plans a **side business** to buy time.
She's pragmatic, blames nobody, and wants **cheap loans** and courses that fit around milking.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her shop work, her goat work and Steve's plastering would all go fast.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small-business loans** and courses that fit around **milking**.
